1.why: All four answer different plausible utterances (clarify depot / renegotiate time / give directions / confirm meeting). Picked D only because it carries the most back-reference ('then', 'ticket window'), which is a shape heuristic, not evidence.

2.why: C is the only option that handles a third party's claim the way an office actually would (needs it in writing from him). B, D and A are all competent replies to nearby utterances, so nothing is truly eliminable.

3.why: D is the only option that accepts a specific proposed time and adds a condition; the others are commentary, over-concession, or a counter-proposal. All remain sayable, so no eliminations.

4.why: Conceding-with-a-caveat (copy thesis off first) fits a 'we need to wipe/take your machine' utterance, but B/C/D each fit a different plausible utterance equally well.

5.why: C is the only compliance reply with anaphora tying to both the objects ('them') and a movement the speaker was already making ('before I head up'). D (receipt roll) is odd but sayable to 'anything else before we open?'.

6.why: Section moved off Thursday. Accepting (A) and pushing back (D) are both fully natural; genuinely 50/50 without the utterance.

7.why: Housing offer; conditional acceptance is key-shaped, but 'is it for the year?' and 'can I move later?' are equally competent first replies.

8.why: Denying ownership ('that car sold in the spring') is the strongest content reply, but A/B/D all work against slightly different utterances. A reads slightly muddled (appeal + offering to pay) but is not incoherent.

9.why: Laundry/lounge setting; C accommodates a request to spread out and matches the physical detail. B and D are equally serviceable replies to a booking claim.

10.why: C is the only option that corrects a misreading of the email (confirmation, not cancellation), which is the discriminating move; the others presuppose the cancellation is real.

11.why: Staff taking the machine out of service is the responsible reply, but 'log it at the front desk' is an equally competent staff reply and D is a plausible peer remark.

12.why: A corrects the customer's false premise (an emailed/phone file never touched a scanner). Eliminated B: 'which of our machines did you actually watch it come off' presumes the customer stood watching the print, which no print-shop staffer would ask.

13.why: B is the most operationally specific staff reply (bad machine, move desks, restore draft), but A's 'it's only the screen lock' is an equally good premise-correction.

14.why: Register + repair: voiding a rental and re-ringing as a purchase is the only option that fixes a transaction already in progress; the others answer pre-sale or post-sale utterances.

15.why: C is the only option that both rejects the offered timeline and proposes an alternative, and it names the constraint (Monday) the other options ignore.

16.why: Classic wrong-party deflection: doc access has to come from whoever created it. The others assume access is not the issue.

17.why: Asking whether the loop still reaches Hale in time is the natural follow-up to a route change, but A/B/D each answer a slightly different version of that utterance.

18.why: Mailroom; 'check behind the counter for mine' follows from an oversize-parcel utterance, but A and D are equally competent.

19.why: B is the only reply that both explains the failure and resolves the customer's immediate problem. C's 'ten minutes before lunch rush' is odd but defensible as a load complaint, so not eliminable.

20.why: Eliminated B: option D establishes that Friday IS a deadline, so agreeing to hold the form until after Friday is agreeing to miss it — self-defeating regardless of the utterance. A is the coherent submit-now-amend-later move.

21.why: Writing-centre script: the student keeps authorship and asks the tutor to flag drift. Eliminated B: 'my professor sets the thesis wording in her office hours' is not something a competent student says about their own thesis to anyone.

22.why: Clarifying scope (log vs readings) is key-shaped, but offering a delivery time or mentioning the pencil pages are both natural.

23.why: Declining-with-reason fits a 'can I keep this slip' utterance; granting it (A) fits equally well and I cannot tell who holds the slip.

24.why: Conditional agreement to enter the counts is the cooperative reply; A's data-validity caveat is an equally plausible key and I have no way to choose.

25.why: 'I'll leave it with them' fits 'I already reported it to maintenance'; D fits 'it's still broken'. Coin flip.

26.why: Lending the card with a condition. D (declining) is equally natural; C is shady but is still something a friend says, so not eliminable on competence.

27.why: B is the only option that corrects a mis-assignment rather than working around it, and two other options (C, D) presuppose the same mismatch, which points at an error in the utterance.

28.why: Declining Friday with a clinical conflict is key-shaped, but A, B and D are all natural replies to a 'let the plumber in Friday' utterance.

29.why: After unanswered voicemails, redirecting to the person who actually holds the sheet is the only reply that changes the outcome. B repeats the failed channel and D is a fine grumble, so neither is strictly eliminable.

30.why: Refusing to sign on someone else's behalf is the standard key. A is filling in a name rather than forging a signature, so it stays sayable.

31.why: Agreeing to a day for a specific part is the fullest integration, but 'I already picked it up' and the clarifying question are both competent.

32.why: C is the only conditional agreement about stock quantity, which is what a print request needs. B's ink claim is dubious print lore but people say it, so it survives.
